title: sim: 33 duplicate questions rewritten into new questions from the same lessons, and 2 capstone prompts reworded to fit their keys

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m01-what-a-deck-is ord 4 (why the six sections are in a fixed order)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test why SOLUTION must follow PROPS, from lesson m01 l02; the module question keeps the single-pass idea.

prompt.old: Why must the six deck sections appear in a fixed order?
prompt.new: Why can the SOLUTION section not be placed before PROPS in a deck?

explanation.old: RUNSPEC declares dimensions so GRID can be checked, GRID establishes cells so PROPS has something to apply to, PROPS defines fluids so SOLUTION can equilibrate, and SOLUTION sets the state SCHEDULE starts from. Nothing goes back to reinterpret an earlier section.
explanation.new: SOLUTION puts the fluids where gravity would have put them, and that integration needs the fluid densities and PVT that PROPS defines. A simulator reads a deck in a single pass and never goes back. The grid dimensions come from RUNSPEC, and the contacts and datum sit in SOLUTION's own EQUIL line.

0.old: Because the sections are stored as separate records and the file's index assumes them in that sequence.
0.new: Because PROPS declares the grid dimensions that SOLUTION sizes its arrays by, and a simulator cannot allocate cells it has not yet been told about.

1.old: Because a simulator reads a deck in a single pass, so each section depends on the ones before it having been read already.
1.new: Because SOLUTION equilibrates the fluids under gravity, which needs the densities and PVT tables that PROPS defines.

2.old: Because reordering them changes which defaults apply, since a default is taken from the most recently read section.
2.new: Because PROPS carries the contacts and the datum, and SOLUTION needs both of them to assign each cell a fluid.

3.old: Because the format was standardised before random access was practical, so the ordering is historical rather than functional.
3.new: It can be; the order is only a convention, and a simulator reading SOLUTION first returns to PROPS later.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m02-the-grid ord 3 (what the half-cell origin offset buys)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test where the grid places Ekene-2, the well that misses the lattice, from lesson m02 l01.

prompt.old: The deck's origin is half a cell south-west of the field's map origin. What does that achieve?
prompt.new: Ekene-2 is posted at (2200, 1150). Where does the block-centred grid place it?

explanation.old: A well on a boundary belongs to two cells and needs a tie-break, and tie-breaks differ between tools. Ekene-1 at (1000, 1000) sits at the centre of cell (11, 11) because of the offset, while Ekene-2 at a northing of 1150 m does not, which the Professional tier takes up.
explanation.new: With the offset, cell (i, j) is centred at (i - 1) x 100 m east and (j - 1) x 100 m north, so a well on multiples of 100 m lands on a centre. 1150 is not a multiple of 100, so Ekene-2 falls in cell (23, 13) with its centre at 1200 m. The well index does not move a well within its cell, and the Professional tier measures what the offset costs.

0.old: It removes the need to transform coordinates between the map frame and the deck frame at all.
0.new: Exactly on a cell centre, because the half-cell offset of the deck's origin puts every Ekene well on one.

1.old: It centres the accumulation in the grid so the structure is symmetric about the model's middle.
1.new: Across the boundary between two cells, with its connections shared equally between the cells either side.

2.old: A well at map coordinates that are multiples of 100 m lands on a cell centre rather than on a boundary.
2.new: In cell (23, 13), whose centre is at a northing of 1200 m, so the well sits half a cell from where the grid places it.

3.old: It aligns the model with the seismic bin grid, which is conventionally offset by half a bin from the map grid.
3.new: In cell (23, 13), with its well index adjusted for the well's true position so that the grid carries it exactly where it was posted.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m02-the-grid ord 7 (how the deck carries net-to-gross)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test where the one-tenth kv/kh ratio comes from, from lesson m02 l03.

prompt.old: The Ekene deck has no NTG keyword. How is net-to-gross carried?
prompt.new: In every Ekene layer the vertical permeability is one tenth of the horizontal. Where does that ratio come from?

explanation.old: The alternative is a gross thickness of about 43 ft with an NTG applied separately, and both give the same pore volume. They give different depths to every interface below layer 1, so a deck must state which convention it uses because nothing about the numbers reveals it.
explanation.new: The lesson states the one-tenth ratio as a design constant of the deck. The Dykstra-Parsons fit concerns the spread of horizontal permeability between the layers, and the net-to-gross is carried in the thicknesses. Real kv/kh ratios run from 0.01 to 1 and are rarely measured directly.

0.old: In the layer thicknesses, which are already net pay, combined with a porosity of 0.2 that is the porosity of net rock.
0.new: It is a design constant of this deck; real fields have a kv/kh between 0.01 and 1, and it is rarely measured directly.

1.old: In the porosity, which is the gross value already multiplied by the net-to-gross of 0.8.
1.new: From the SCAL course's core plugs, which measured vertical and horizontal permeability on each layer.

2.old: In the permeability, which is scaled down so that the layer's flow capacity comes out correct in spite of the gross thickness used.
2.new: From the waterflood course's Dykstra-Parsons column, whose log-normal fit to the five layers fixes the vertical permeability at a tenth of the horizontal.

3.old: It is not carried at all, which is the reason the deck's pore volume exceeds the volumetric booking's.
3.new: From the net-to-gross of 0.8, which scales down the vertical flow capacity of each layer.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m02-the-grid ord 9 (which GRID block does not compress)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test why compressed blocks give reviewable diffs, from lesson m02 l04.

prompt.old: Which block in Ekene's GRID section does not compress, and what does that tell you?
prompt.new: When a deck is kept under version control, why do compressed blocks make its changes easier to review?

explanation.old: PORO, PERMX, PERMY and PERMZ are all layer-constant and compress to five tokens each. TOPS is 900 distinct values and is most of the section's length. That diagnostic works on any deck: the incompressible blocks are where the modelling effort went.
explanation.new: The lesson gives two reasons deck size matters, review and diffs. A layer-constant block such as PERMX compresses to one token per layer, so editing one layer's value changes one token, while the same edit in an expanded block touches 900 lines. Line wrapping has no meaning to the simulator either way.

0.old: PERMX, because permeability differs between the five layers rather than being constant across the grid.
0.new: Because version control stores a repeat count natively and records only the count when a value changes.

1.old: PORO, because porosity was populated cell by cell from a geostatistical property model.
1.new: Because a compressed block is read faster, so each committed version can be test-run before review.

2.old: TOPS, because every column has its own depth, and the blocks that resist compression are the ones carrying real spatial variation.
2.new: Because a change to one layer's permeability is then a one-token edit in the block, where an expanded block would show a 900-line change.

3.old: DZ, because layer thickness varies with the structure and therefore differs from column to column.
3.new: Because compression removes the line wrapping, and wrapping is what makes most deck diffs unreadable.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m03-the-tables ord 1 (what the five PROPS keywords have in common)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what the DENSITY value for oil is, from lesson m03 l01.

prompt.old: What do DENSITY, PVTO, PVDG, PVTW and ROCK have in common?
prompt.new: Ekene's DENSITY block gives oil at 54.02790214067278 lb/ft3. What is that number?

explanation.old: A deck contains no correlations. PVTW and ROCK are lines of constants rather than tables, none is optional for a live-oil model, and DENSITY covers all three phases at once. What they share is that they are values, and their provenance lives outside the file.
explanation.new: DENSITY carries the three phases at surface conditions, from gravities of 32 API for oil, 1.03 for brine and 0.75 for gas. The simulator combines them with the formation volume factors to get the reservoir densities that drive segregation and the contacts. Dividing 64.30084 by 1.2 does not give the deck's oil density.

0.old: Each hands the simulator numbers rather than a correlation, so the choice of correlation stays with whoever wrote the deck.
0.new: The surface density that follows from the oil's 32 API gravity, which the simulator combines with Bo to get reservoir density.

1.old: Each is indexed by pressure, so the simulator interpolates all five identically between their rows.
1.new: The reservoir density at the initial 3200 psia, which the simulator divides by Bo to recover a surface value.

2.old: Each is optional, since a simulator falls back on internal correlations for any block absent from the deck.
2.new: The water density of 64.30084 lb/ft3 divided by the oil formation volume factor of 1.2, which is how the deck states the oil's buoyancy against brine.

3.old: Each describes a single phase, so a three-phase model needs exactly three of them and the remaining two exist only for reporting.
3.new: The density measured on the Material Balance course's bottom-hole sample, at reservoir conditions.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m04-initialisation ord 5 (how a cell straddling the contact is treated)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what a 10 ft deeper contact does to the crest column and the oil area, from lesson m04 l02.

prompt.old: How is a cell straddling the contact treated?
prompt.new: Ekene's crest oil column is about 62 ft. What does moving the contact 10 ft deeper do?

explanation.old: There is no partial cell. The staircase's tread is a cell and its riser is a layer thickness, and that roughness is exactly what the Professional tier's volumetric reconciliation measures against the booking.
explanation.new: 10 ft on a 62 ft crest column is about a sixth. A deeper contact also brings more columns into the oil leg, so the area grows by more than the column does. The datum and its pressure are a separate pair. Contacts are usually the most uncertain input and the cheapest to change, which is why a contact sensitivity is standard practice.

0.old: Partially, with saturation proportional to the fraction of the cell lying above the contact depth.
0.new: It raises the pressure at the datum by the water gradient over 10 ft, and leaves the oil in place unchanged.

1.old: Entirely oil or entirely water depending on which side its centre falls, so the modelled contact is a staircase.
1.new: It adds roughly a sixth to the column at the crest, and more than that in area, as more columns come into the oil leg.

2.old: As a transition cell, with saturations interpolated from the capillary pressure curve across the whole of its own thickness.
2.new: It adds roughly a sixth to the column at the crest and leaves the oil area unchanged, because the area is fixed by the TOPS surface alone.

3.old: It is subdivided automatically so the contact can be represented at the depth where it actually falls.
3.new: It adds 10 ft to the crest column out of 161 ft of relief, about six percent, with the area unchanged.

items.flag: exact-key duplicate of beginner module m04-initialisation ord 14 (the no-well first check)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test why a state at rest is an assumption, from lesson m04 l04.

prompt.old: What is the standard first check on a new deck's initialisation?
prompt.new: Equilibration asserts that the model starts at rest. Why is that an assumption rather than an observation?

explanation.old: If the initial state is not in equilibrium the model moves with no wells open, and the drift looks like a physical response. The usual culprits are a density inconsistent with the PVT tables or a contact outside the grid. Comparing against the booking is also worth doing and tests something different.
explanation.new: Equilibrium means every phase pressure gradient is balanced by gravity, so nothing moves. A real field at discovery need not be in that state, and a deck that equilibrates has assumed regional flow, tilted contacts and active aquifers away. The zero capillary pressures only remove the transition zone.

0.old: Compare the reported oil in place against the booking, which is the only test of whether the contact is right.
0.new: Because pressure is only measured after production starts, so the state at time zero is never observed at all.

1.old: Run it with no wells for a short period and confirm nothing changes; a pressure drift means the initialisation and the property fields disagree.
1.new: Because a real reservoir at discovery may have regional flow, tilted contacts or an active aquifer sweeping across it, and equilibrating assumes them all away.

2.old: Confirm the datum lies within the grid's depth range, since a datum outside it cannot be integrated from.
2.new: Because the simulator cannot compute flow at time zero, so rest is imposed until the first well opens.

3.old: Check the equilibration iteration count in the log, which rises sharply when the initial state is inconsistent.
3.new: Because zero capillary pressure forces every phase to be stationary, whatever the reservoir was doing.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m05-wells-and-schedule ord 9 (report steps against solver steps)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test why frequent control changes cost run time, from lesson m05 l03.

prompt.old: A DATES entry defines a report step. What is its relationship to the solver's own steps?
prompt.new: Why is a history-matching deck that changes well controls every month more expensive to run than one that changes them yearly?

explanation.old: Ekene's 36 history entries are 36 points at which results are written rather than 36 solves. Report steps cost output volume and nothing else; a tiny report interval buys a larger file and the same answer.
explanation.new: Report steps cost output volume and solver steps cost run time. A control change forces the solver to cut its step and rebuild, so a deck with a change every month costs more even when the physics is identical. The 36 history entries are 36 points where results are written rather than 36 solves.

0.old: None directly: the solver chooses its own step size adaptively and may take many internal steps inside one report step.
0.new: Because each abrupt control change forces the solver to cut its step and rebuild, so frequent changes cost run time.

1.old: They coincide one for one, so refining the report interval is how a modeller reduces the time-discretisation error of the solution.
1.new: Because every DATES entry is a separate solve, so 36 monthly entries mean 36 solves where a yearly schedule needs only three.

2.old: The report step bounds the solver step, so a shorter report interval forces shorter solver steps everywhere and therefore more accuracy.
2.new: Because each report step writes the full state of every cell, and that output volume is what dominates the run time of a history match.

3.old: The solver takes a fixed number of internal steps per report step, configurable through a RUNSPEC option.
3.new: Because WCONHIST rates are re-read from the ledger at every internal step.

items.flag: near duplicate of beginner module m06-the-associate-reading ord 14 (two thirds of the deck is SCHEDULE); module m01 ord 5 carries the same point
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what a tiny PROPS section suggests, from the reading habit in lesson m01 l02.

prompt.old: Two thirds of the Ekene deck is SCHEDULE. What does that say about the study?
prompt.new: When you open an unfamiliar deck, what does a very small PROPS section suggest?

explanation.old: A deck that is nearly all GRID is a big static model with a short run; one with a tiny PROPS section is probably using defaults worth checking. Ekene's GRID section is short because its properties are constant and compress, and its PROPS section is a full set of tables.
explanation.new: The reading habit is to find the six section headers and note their line ranges first. A deck that is nearly all SCHEDULE is a history-matched study, one that is nearly all GRID is a big static model, and one with a tiny PROPS section is probably using defaults. A deck hands the simulator numbers rather than correlations, and PROPS tables do not grow with the grid.

0.old: It has an unusually detailed grid, since the completions for every well are written into the schedule.
0.new: That the fluid is dead oil, since a live oil would need a PVTO table carrying one record per solution gas ratio.

1.old: It was generated rather than hand-written, since a hand-written deck would balance its sections more evenly.
1.new: That the fluid is described by a correlation, which the simulator evaluates internally from a handful of gravities.

2.old: It carries a long production history, which is what a history-matched study looks like from the outside.
2.new: That the deck is probably relying on defaults, which you should go and check before trusting its fluids.

3.old: It is largely defaulted elsewhere, which is why the sections carrying explicit data look disproportionately large.
3.new: That the model has few cells, since PROPS grows with the grid.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m01-where-the-structure-comes-from ord 2 (the three decisions an interpolator makes)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what the sill does to the estimate, from lesson m01 l02.

prompt.old: Which three things must an interpolator decide that the data does not determine?
prompt.new: Ekene's kriging carries a sill of 400. What does changing the sill alone do to the deck's depths?

explanation.old: Range, regional behaviour and exactness at the data. None is determined by six depths and each visibly changes the map. Cell size and layering are gridding decisions downstream of the surface.
explanation.new: The sill is the variance the surface reaches at large separation. On its own it does not change the estimate, because it appears in both the weights and the system they solve, and it matters only for the uncertainty, which this deck does not carry. The range sets how far influence reaches and the nugget decides whether the surface passes through the data.

0.old: How far a well's influence reaches, what the surface does far from any well, and whether it passes exactly through the data.
0.new: Nothing to the estimate, since the sill scales the covariance in both the weights and the system they solve; it matters for uncertainty.

1.old: The cell size, the number of layers, and the depth reference the finished surface is quoted against in the deck.
1.new: It moves the whole surface toward the regional mean, so a larger sill deepens every column away from the wells.

2.old: Which of the wells to include, how heavily to weight the measurement error carried by each, and where to place the grid origin relative to the map.
2.new: It changes how far each well's influence reaches, so a larger sill spreads every well's measured depth across more of the 900 columns in the deck.

3.old: Whether to grid in time or depth, which velocity model to use, and how to tie the converted surface back to the wells.
3.new: It sets how closely the surface honours each well, so a larger sill lets the map smooth through the tops.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m01-where-the-structure-comes-from ord 6 (the 2.3e-13 m residual)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test when a non-zero nugget is the right choice, from lesson m01 l03.

prompt.old: Two of the exactly-recovered wells carry a residual of about 2.3e-13 m. What is that?
prompt.new: When would a non-zero nugget be the better choice for a surface like Ekene's?

explanation.old: Two tenths of a picometre is arithmetic rather than structure. A discrepancy at the thirteenth decimal is floating point and one at the second is a modelling decision, and knowing which you are looking at is the skill.
explanation.new: A nugget tells the interpolator how much of the scatter to treat as noise. A well top is picked from a log by a person and two people pick differently, so forcing the surface through every pick puts a spurious feature at every well. Ekene uses zero because its six tops are exact by construction.

0.old: The metre to foot and back round trip, because the deck stores depths in feet and the conversion is not exact in binary.
0.new: When the well tops carry pick error, so the surface should pass near the data instead of honouring noise as signal.

1.old: The convergence tolerance of the kriging solve, which stops when successive estimates differ by less than that amount.
1.new: When the wells are further apart than the range, so the surface needs a nugget to carry influence across the gaps between them.

2.old: A genuine structural residual, since simple kriging is only exact in the limit and this nugget is small rather than zero.
2.new: When the deck stores depths in feet, so the nugget can absorb the unit round-trip residual the kriging would otherwise leave.

3.old: The precision of the coordinate transform between the map frame and the deck frame, applied twice in opposite directions.
3.new: When the regional mean is unknown and must be estimated from six points.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m03-fluid-provenance ord 7 (symptom of a deck-only PVT update)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test how the fluid rule inverts when the deck is built first, from lesson m03 l03.

prompt.old: A new PVT report arrives and somebody updates the deck alone. What is the symptom months later?
prompt.new: Occasionally the simulation model is built before the other analyses. What does the fluid rule say then?

explanation.old: The deck runs perfectly and returns different answers. Volumes drift from the booking, the match stops reproducing pressures, and the ledger's factors are stale, and none of it appears as an error.
explanation.new: When the deck is the first thing built, its PVT is the reference and everything else adopts it. What is never acceptable is two authoritative sources, because a tank model on one fluid and a simulation model on another give two answers for the size of the field and no way to choose.

0.old: A model that used to match and no longer does, with no change to the geology, until somebody finds the PVT commit.
0.new: It inverts: the deck's PVT becomes the reference and the other analyses must adopt it, so there is one source.

1.old: A deck that fails to validate, because the new tables disagree with the RSVD value in the SOLUTION section.
1.new: Nothing changes: the deck takes the latest laboratory report and the other analyses follow when revised.

2.old: An error raised at initialisation, since the oil in place the deck reports no longer matches the value carried in the study document.
2.new: The deck carries a correlated fluid until the laboratory report arrives, since no other analysis exists yet that it could be matched against.

3.old: Results that differ between runs, because the two fluid descriptions are being mixed between report steps.
3.new: Each analysis may keep its own fluid, provided the deck records which one it used.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m03-fluid-provenance ord 11 (why the gas is correlated and the oil designed)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what the gas table shows across its pressure range, from lesson m03 l04.

prompt.old: Why is Ekene's gas table correlated while its oil is designed?
prompt.new: Ekene's gas table runs from 400 to 3800 psia. What does it show the gas doing across that range?

explanation.old: The material balance course modelled Ekene as undersaturated, the ledger set the gas factor to zero and the SCAL course worked in oil and water. A correlation on the field's own gas gravity is the honest fallback.
explanation.new: Across the twelve rows Bg falls by a factor of ten and viscosity roughly doubles. That is gas doing what gas does: it compresses hard, and compressed gas is more viscous. The table comes from the Hall and Yarborough z-factor with Lee, Gonzalez and Eakin viscosity on a gas gravity of 0.75.

0.old: Gas properties are insensitive to the correlation chosen, so a correlated gas adds negligible uncertainty to anything.
0.new: Bg rises steadily with pressure while viscosity stays nearly constant, as a dry gas would at 180 F.

1.old: The gas table is only used below the bubble point, which Ekene never reaches, so its provenance does not matter.
1.new: Bg falls by a factor of ten while viscosity roughly halves, as the gas approaches the oil's properties.

2.old: No earlier course built a gas description, so there was nothing to inherit and inventing one would mean designing a fluid nobody would check.
2.new: Bg falls by a factor of ten while the viscosity roughly doubles, because gas compresses hard and compressed gas is more viscous.

3.old: Designing a gas table needs a compositional analysis, which the field's fluid sampling programme never included.
3.new: Bg and viscosity both stay near their bubble-point values, since no free gas forms in Ekene's history.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m04-rock-curves-from-the-lab ord 3 (why the deck carries a table rather than the Corey model)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test how to judge the SWOF row count, from lesson m04 l01.

prompt.old: Why does the deck carry a table rather than the Corey model?
prompt.new: Ekene's SWOF carries 22 rows. What is a useful test of whether that row count is enough?

explanation.old: That is a deliberate design: it keeps the simulator independent of any particular saturation model, at the cost of losing the provenance at the boundary. The same trade appears throughout PROPS.
explanation.new: The row count is a judgement: too few and the polyline departs from the curve, too many and the table is decoration. A sensitivity on the count is the direct test. Twenty two uniformly spaced rows is fine for a curve this smooth.

0.old: Because a table is faster to evaluate at run time than a power law would be at every timestep of the run.
0.new: Check that the rows bracket the full saturation range, since the end rows decide the interpolation.

1.old: Because the format has no way to express a saturation model: every simulator interpolates rows and there is no keyword for Corey.
1.new: Halve the row count and see whether anything downstream moves; if nothing does, the original count was generous.

2.old: Because simulators implement Corey differently, so a table is the only portable way to state the same curve.
2.new: Use one row per percent of mobile saturation, which is the standard resolution for a Corey table.

3.old: Because the model was fitted to laboratory points and the table is those points rather than the fit through them.
3.new: Confirm the rows reproduce the six Corey parameters exactly when a curve is fitted back.

items.flag: exact-key duplicate of intermediate module m04-rock-curves-from-the-lab ord 4 (the four numbers that set scale)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what a higher residual oil costs in movable oil, from lesson m04 l02.

prompt.old: Which four numbers set the scale of the displacement rather than its shape?
prompt.new: Ekene's residual oil is 0.25. What would a value of 0.30 do?

explanation.old: Connate water sets the oil in place, residual oil sets the maximum displacement efficiency, and the endpoint mobilities set the mobility ratio. Everything between them is shape, which the exponents control.
explanation.new: The movable oil is one minus connate water minus residual oil, 0.4 of the pore space at a residual of 0.25. Raising the residual by 0.05 removes 0.05 of that 0.4, which is an eighth. The two curves look nearly identical over most of their range and differ only where they stop, which is why endpoint errors hide.

0.old: Connate water, residual oil and the two endpoint mobilities.
0.new: Remove an eighth of the movable oil from the field.

1.old: The two Corey exponents and the two endpoint mobilities, since exponents give curvature and endpoints give magnitude.
1.new: Leave the movable oil unchanged, since residual oil only moves the curve's end point and not the volume that can be displaced.

2.old: The first and last rows of each table, which bracket the range every interior row is interpolated within.
2.new: Remove a twentieth of the movable oil, since the residual rises by 0.05 on a total pore space of one.

3.old: Connate water, residual oil, the row count and the row spacing, which set both the range and its resolution.
3.new: Raise the water endpoint mobility, since the table must reach its krw endpoint at a lower water saturation.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m04-rock-curves-from-the-lab ord 10 (what one saturation region assumes)
items.reason: Final copy rewritten to test what the zero Pc column leaves out of the SCAL work, from lesson m04 l04.

prompt.old: One saturation region across five layers spanning a factor of six in permeability. What does that assume?
prompt.new: Ekene's tables carry zero capillary pressure. What did the SCAL course build that the deck leaves out?

explanation.old: Pore structure is what makes one layer 600 md and another 100. Simulators support multiple regions for exactly this reason, and this deck uses one because the SCAL course fitted one curve.
explanation.new: The SCAL course built a real capillary pressure curve for this sand from a Leverett J-function and used it to show that the crest is drier than the flanks. None of that is in the deck. For a field with 49 m of relief and a transition zone of a few metres that is a reasonable simplification, and the study should say so.

0.old: That pore structure, and so the shape of the relative permeability curves, is the same in the 607 md layer as in the 102 md one.
0.new: A Leverett J-function capillary curve showing the crest drier than the flanks, a fair omission for a thin transition zone.

prompt.old: Ekene has six wells and 900 grid columns. What does that ratio say about the model's structure?
prompt.new: What is the tell that a deck's structure is a flat placeholder nobody replaced?

explanation.old: That is the normal condition of every reservoir model ever built, and saying it out loud is the point. The deck carries no uncertainty at all, and the wells were placed by drilling history rather than by a sampling design.
explanation.new: Setting every column top to the average of the six wells gives a flat grid whose contact includes everything or nothing. It happens as a placeholder that nobody replaced, and the tell is a TOPS block that compresses to one repeat count. Exactness at the wells is what a zero-nugget interpolator does anyway.

0.old: That the model is under-constrained and its structure should not be used for volumetrics until more wells are drilled.
0.new: A crest that sits exactly on a mapped well top, since an exact interpolator puts it there.

1.old: That the six wells were placed to sample the structure evenly, which is why the interpolation between them is reliable.
1.new: A datum depth equal to the contact, which the equilibration forces for a flat grid.

2.old: That 894 of the 900 column depths are interpolated, so the structure of the model is a hypothesis carrying only six anchors.
2.new: A TOPS block that compresses to a single repeat count, because every column then carries the same depth.

3.old: That the interpolation carries an estimation variance the deck records alongside each column, which is how the structural uncertainty is propagated forward.
3.new: A TOPS block holding exactly six distinct values, one per mapped well, repeated across the columns nearest to each well.

prompt.old: A learner submits 1565 m as the depth the model carries at Ekene-2. What have they read?
prompt.new: A learner submits 1565 m for capstone field 4, the depth the model carries at Ekene-2. What mistake produced that?

explanation.old: The check is that the answer should be shallower than 1565 and by less than a metre. If it equals 1565 exactly you have read the well database rather than the deck. Reading the kriged value at the well's own position is the same mistake seen from the other side, and it is the reason it happens.
explanation.new: The check is that the answer should be shallower than 1565 and by less than a metre. If it equals 1565 exactly you have read the well database rather than the deck. The deck samples the surface at the centre of cell (23, 13), 50 m north of the well, which is why its depth differs from the mapped top.

2.old: Reporting the kriged value at the well's exact position, which is 1565 m and is what an exact interpolator must return there.
2.new: Reporting the depth at the centre of cell (23, 13), 50 m north of the well, which is where the grid samples the surface.
